_meta.name: Casebook
_meta.note: One shape for every alert. 'depth' says whether opening it buys anything: shallow cases are resolved on the file in front of you, deep ones have lines of enquiry that cost hours. The shift decides how deep to go, not the data.

cases.title: Six cash deposits in eleven days
cases.customer: Retail · Ms L. Peeters · customer since 2011 · low risk
cases.narrative: Six cash deposits of between €8,000 and €9,600, all at branch counters, over eleven days. No prior cash activity of any size on this account in fourteen years.
cases.on_file: No supporting documentation on file. Relationship manager has not been contacted.

flags.text: Amounts consistently below the €10,000 cash reporting threshold
Sharp departure from a fourteen-year behavioural baseline
Deposits split across two branches
No known adverse media or sanctions nexus

cases.law: AMLR Art. 69 — occasional transactions above €10,000; Art. 25 — ongoing monitoring
cases.why: This looks exactly like structuring, and it may well be. But there is a mundane explanation that fits equally well — an inheritance, a car sale, cash gifts at a wedding — and you have not asked. Escalating now sends investigations a case with no source-of-funds question posed; closing it ignores a textbook pattern. The correct first move is cheap: ask.

consequences.close: You closed a textbook structuring pattern without asking a single question. If this was laundering, the file shows an analyst who saw the pattern and did nothing.
consequences.escalate: Defensible, but you spent two investigator days on a question a five-minute call might have answered. Do this across a queue and the real cases wait behind it.
consequences.rfi: Right. Source of funds first, decision second.

cases.title: Salary account suddenly forwarding funds
cases.customer: Retail · Mr D. Okonkwo · customer since 2024 · standard risk
cases.narrative: Twelve inbound transfers from unrelated private individuals, each €2,900–€4,600, followed within hours by outbound transfers to three accounts abroad. Balance returns to near zero each time.
cases.on_file: Customer is 21, opened the account for a student job. No business activity declared. Two inbound senders appear in an internal fraud-victim list.

flags.text: Pass-through: funds in and straight out, balance returns to zero
Activity wholly inconsistent with a declared student profile
Inbound senders unrelated to each other and to the customer
Two senders already flagged as fraud victims

cases.law: AMLR Art. 25 — ongoing monitoring; Art. 69 — reporting of suspicious transactions
cases.why: This is a money mule account and the fraud-victim match makes it close to certain. Pass-through behaviour on a young account with no economic rationale is one of the clearest patterns there is. Asking the customer here is not neutral — it risks tipping off, and the answer would not change what the transaction record already shows.

consequences.close: A live mule account left running. Victim funds continued to move through it.
consequences.escalate: Correct, and quickly. This is what the escalation route exists for.
consequences.rfi: You delayed a near-certain mule case to ask a question the data already answered — and contacting the customer risks tipping off.

cases.title: €180,000 to a notary
cases.customer: Retail · Mr & Mrs Vandenberghe · customers since 2003 · low risk
cases.narrative: A single transfer of €180,000 to a Belgian notary account, referenced with a property address. Funded by the closure of a savings account held at the same bank since 2009.
cases.on_file: Savings account shows fourteen years of regular monthly contributions. Mortgage application with this bank was approved two weeks earlier for the same address.

flags.text: Source of funds fully visible and internally verifiable
Counterparty is a regulated notary, not an opaque third party
Corroborated by an approved mortgage on the same property
Amount is a large deviation from monthly baseline

cases.law: AMLR Art. 20 — CDD proportionate to risk; Art. 34 — EDD only where higher risk is present
cases.why: The rule fired on size alone, and size alone is not suspicion. Everything here reconciles: fourteen years of savings, a notary counterparty, a mortgage file in the same institution for the same address. This is the 95% of the queue that is noise — and closing it confidently, with a recorded rationale, is a skill in its own right. Analysts who cannot close cleanly escalate everything, and then nothing gets investigated properly.

consequences.escalate: Two investigator days spent on a documented house purchase. Multiply that across a queue and the genuinely suspicious cases sit in a backlog.
consequences.rfi: You asked for information the bank already holds — the mortgage file is internal.

cases.title: Trade payments routed through three countries
cases.customer: Corporate · Meridian Trading BVBA · customer since 2019 · high risk
cases.narrative: Four payments for machinery parts, invoiced by a UAE intermediary, with goods shipped directly from Pakistan to Belgium. Invoice values are 40–60% above comparable market pricing.
cases.on_file: Gulf Machinery FZE was incorporated four months ago. Beneficial owner not established — corporate shareholder in a jurisdiction with no public register. Goods never enter the UAE.

flags.text: Intermediary adds no logistical function — goods bypass it entirely
Invoice pricing materially above market
Counterparty incorporated four months ago
Beneficial ownership of the counterparty not established

cases.law: AMLR Art. 34 — EDD where no apparent economic purpose; Art. 22 — beneficial ownership
cases.why: Classic trade-based laundering: an intermediary that handles no goods, over-invoicing that moves value rather than merchandise, and a counterparty whose owner you cannot identify. Any one of these would warrant a question. Together they are a case. Note that this customer was already rated high risk — which should have meant enhanced monitoring, not a routine alert.

consequences.close: You closed a trade-based laundering pattern on a high-risk customer.
consequences.escalate: Correct. Note the beneficial ownership gap — that alone required action.
consequences.rfi: Reasonable instinct, but you already have enough: three independent red flags on a customer rated high risk. Asking delays a case that is already made.

cases.title: Dormant account wakes up with a round sum
cases.customer: Retail · Mr S. Haddad · customer since 2016 · standard risk
cases.narrative: A single inbound transfer of €25,000 from a French bank, reference "prêt familial". No subsequent activity. Funds remain in the account.
transactions: from Crédit Mutuel, ref: prêt familial
cases.on_file: Sender name matches the customer’s surname. Customer address updated to France in 2021. No adverse media. Funds have not moved.

flags.text: Sender shares the customer surname — consistent with a family loan
Funds have not moved on; no layering behaviour
Sending institution is an EU regulated bank
Account reactivation after long dormancy

cases.law: AMLR Art. 20 — purpose and intended nature of the relationship
cases.why: Dormancy rules generate enormous noise. Here the reactivation has a coherent story: the customer moved to France, and a same-surname sender at a regulated French bank transferred a stated family loan that has not moved since. Nothing layers, nothing structures. Escalating this is defensible but wasteful; the discipline is to write the rationale down and close it.

consequences.close: Right. Coherent explanation, no layering, rationale recorded.
consequences.escalate: Understandable caution, but capacity spent on a family transfer that never moved.
consequences.rfi: Not unreasonable — but everything you would ask is already visible on the file.

cases.title: Three accounts, one pattern
cases.customer: Retail · Three unrelated customers, same branch · all standard risk

facts.Profile: Three individual accounts, no declared connection

cases.narrative: Three customers with no declared relationship each deposited cash on the same three dates, at the same branch, in amounts between €4,500 and €6,200 — then each transferred the balance to a single fourth account within 48 hours.
cases.on_file: The receiving account belongs to a company whose director is the brother of customer A. The company is a car dealership.

flags.text: Coordinated timing across supposedly unrelated parties
Amounts individually below any single-transaction trigger
Rapid consolidation into one controlled account
Undisclosed familial link to the receiving entity

cases.law: AMLR Art. 69 — structuring is reportable; Art. 22 — control relationships
cases.why: The individual deposits are unremarkable. The pattern is the case. Structuring detection is about aggregation across parties, and the undisclosed family link to the receiving company removes the innocent reading. This is exactly the case that gets missed when analysts work alerts one account at a time instead of looking across them.

consequences.close: A coordinated structuring ring left in place.
consequences.escalate: Correct — and note you had to look across three alerts to see it.
consequences.rfi: You have four converging flags and an undisclosed relationship. Asking delays a case that is already sufficient.

cases.title: A 78% name match on a designated person
cases.customer: Retail · Mr A. Kuznetsov · customer since 2018 · standard risk
cases.narrative: Screening flagged the customer against a designated individual on the EU consolidated list at 78% fuzzy match. The alert relates to a routine €2,300 rent payment.
cases.on_file: Designated person: Aleksei KUZNETSOV, born 1961, Russian national, resident Moscow. Customer: Anton KUZNETSOV, born 1989, Belgian national, born in Ghent, holds Belgian ID verified at onboarding. Different date of birth, different first name, different nationality.

flags.text: Date of birth, first name and nationality all differ from the designated person
Identity verified against a Belgian ID document at onboarding
Payment is a long-standing routine standing order
Surname matches a designated individual

cases.law: EU Regulation 269/2014 — asset freeze obligations; AMLR Art. 20 — CDD proportionate to risk
cases.why: Sanctions screening produces enormous fuzzy-match noise, and the discipline is to resolve the match on identifiers rather than on the name. Here three independent identifiers diverge: first name, date of birth and nationality. This is a false positive and should be closed with the discriminating data recorded — that record is what stops the same alert consuming time every month.

consequences.close: Right. And recording which identifiers discriminated is what prevents this alert recurring forever.
consequences.escalate: Sanctions hits feel dangerous to close, which is exactly why they clog queues. Three identifiers differ; escalating this spends capacity and teaches the screening system nothing.
consequences.rfi: You asked for information already on the file — the verified Belgian ID answers this.

cases.title: Inbound from an exchange, onward to a private wallet
cases.customer: Retail · Ms N. Ferreira · customer since 2022 · standard risk
cases.narrative: Four inbound transfers from a crypto exchange registered in Estonia, then onward transfers to two accounts the customer has not previously used. Chain analytics on the originating addresses shows indirect exposure to a sanctioned mixing service two hops back.
cases.on_file: Customer declared crypto trading as a side activity at onboarding in 2022. Volumes then were under €5,000 a year. No source-of-wealth documentation on file. Travel-rule originator data absent on three of the four inbound transfers.

flags.text: Indirect exposure to a sanctioned mixing service
Volumes roughly twenty times the declared activity level
Travel-rule originator information missing on most transfers
Immediate onward transfer to previously unused accounts

cases.law: TFR (EU) 2023/1113 Art. 14 — missing originator information; AMLR Art. 34(4) — source of funds and wealth
cases.why: Mixer exposure alone justifies enhanced scrutiny, but the decisive fact is the combination: sanctioned-service exposure, a twentyfold departure from declared activity, and absent travel-rule data. Missing originator information is not an administrative gap under the TFR — it is itself a trigger. Asking the customer risks tipping off and would not change what the chain analytics already establish.

consequences.close: You closed a case with sanctioned-mixer exposure and missing travel-rule data.
consequences.escalate: Correct. Note that the missing originator data was independently sufficient.
consequences.rfi: You have four converging flags including sanctions exposure. Asking delays a made case and risks tipping off.

cases.title: A mayor's spouse opens a savings account
cases.customer: Retail · Mrs C. Lemaire · new customer · PEP-related

facts.Profile: Retired teacher, spouse of a municipal mayor

cases.narrative: Screening identified the customer as the spouse of a domestic PEP — mayor of a Belgian municipality of 18,000 inhabitants. Initial funding of €35,000 transferred from a joint account held at another Belgian bank.
transactions: joint account, KBC — same customer name
cases.on_file: Source of funds: proceeds of a property sale, notarial deed provided at onboarding. Senior management approval for the PEP relationship was NOT obtained. Source of wealth documented. No adverse media.

flags.text: Senior management approval for a PEP relationship was never obtained
Source of funds documented by notarial deed
Funds transferred from an account in the customer's own name
No adverse media or corruption indicators

cases.law: AMLR Art. 42 — politically exposed persons; requires senior management approval, source of wealth, and enhanced ongoing monitoring
cases.why: The transaction is not suspicious — the money is documented and comes from her own account. But PEP status carries a procedural obligation that has been missed: Art. 42 requires senior management approval before establishing the relationship, and it was never obtained. This is the case that teaches an important distinction: not every alert is about laundering. Some are about your own control failing. Closing this hides a compliance gap; escalating to investigations sends it to the wrong team. It goes back for the approval.

consequences.close: You closed it as a false positive — which the transaction was. But you also closed a live gap: no senior management approval exists for a PEP relationship. An examiner would find that.
consequences.escalate: Investigations will find no suspicion here, because there isn't any. The missing item is a procedural approval, not a case.
consequences.rfi: Right. The transaction is clean; the file is not. Route it back for the Art. 42 approval.

cases.title: A new merchant's volumes triple in a fortnight
cases.customer: Corporate · SunGlow Wellness BV · merchant since Jan 2026 · standard risk
cases.narrative: Card acquiring volume rose from €38,000 in February to €310,000 in the first fortnight of March. Chargeback rate 11%. Average ticket €189 against a projected €45. Cardholder geography spread across 31 countries where the merchant declared Benelux-only sales.
cases.on_file: Merchant declared Benelux-only online sales of supplements at onboarding. Website currently shows a single product page with no stock information. Director appointed three months before onboarding, no prior retail history.

flags.text: Chargeback rate of 11% against a typical retail norm under 1%
Cardholder geography inconsistent with declared Benelux-only sales
Average ticket four times the projected value
Minimal web presence for the volume claimed

cases.law: AMLR Art. 20 — purpose and nature of the business relationship; Art. 25 — ongoing monitoring
cases.why: This is transaction laundering: a merchant account processing payments that are not what they claim to be. The 11% chargeback rate is the giveaway — real retail sits under 1%, and that level of dispute means cardholders do not recognise what they paid for. Combined with geography that contradicts the declared business and a shell-like web presence, this is a case. Payments firms see this pattern far more than banks do.

consequences.close: You left a transaction-laundering merchant processing. Chargeback liability sits with the acquirer.
consequences.escalate: Correct. The chargeback rate alone warranted it.
consequences.rfi: Asking the merchant is reasonable in principle, but an 11% chargeback rate with contradictory geography is already sufficient — and every day of delay is more settlement exposure.

cases.title: A restaurant's takings rise with its bookings
cases.customer: Corporate · Trattoria Lucia BVBA · customer since 2014 · standard risk
cases.narrative: Cash deposits of €96,400 across March against a twelve-month average of €58,000. Deposits made weekly, amounts varying between €18,000 and €27,000, all at the same branch.
cases.on_file: VAT returns filed and consistent with declared turnover. March included Easter weekend and a two-week city food festival. Card takings rose 41% over the same period, proportionate to the cash increase. Same pattern visible in March of the two previous years.

flags.text: Card takings rose proportionately, corroborating genuine trade
Same seasonal pattern in the two prior years
Deposits well above the reporting threshold, not structured beneath it
Cash volume 66% above the twelve-month average

cases.law: AMLR Art. 20 — CDD proportionate to risk; Art. 25 — monitoring against the expected profile
cases.why: Cash-intensive businesses generate constant alerts, and the skill is knowing what corroborates. Here three things do: proportionate card growth, an identical pattern in prior years, and deposits made openly above the threshold rather than structured below it. Note the last point — a launderer structures to avoid reporting; this customer walked in with €27,000. The seasonal explanation is verifiable and verified.

consequences.close: Right, and the corroborating card data is what makes the rationale defensible.
consequences.escalate: Capacity spent on a documented seasonal peak with proportionate card corroboration.
consequences.rfi: Everything you would ask is already on file — VAT returns, card data, and two years of prior pattern.

cases.title: Money that goes around in a circle
cases.customer: Corporate · Novara Consulting BVBA · customer since 2021 · standard risk
cases.narrative: Nine transfers over five weeks. Funds leave the customer to a Luxembourg entity, then to a Cypriot entity, then return to a second Belgian account also held by the customer's director. Each leg carries a consultancy invoice. Net position after five weeks is approximately zero.
cases.on_file: Corporate registry checks show the director of Novara is also a shareholder of Aurex Sàrl. Kestros Ltd beneficial ownership not established — nominee shareholder. No deliverables, contracts or work product on file for any invoice. Total invoiced exceeds the company's entire prior-year turnover.

flags.text: Funds return to an account controlled by the same person — circular flow
Undisclosed common ownership between customer and counterparty
Invoiced amounts exceed the company's entire prior-year turnover
No evidence any service was actually delivered

cases.law: AMLR Art. 34 — EDD where no apparent economic purpose; Art. 22 — beneficial ownership of counterparties
cases.why: Circular flows have no legitimate explanation. Money that leaves and returns to the same controller, carrying invoices for services with no work product, is round-tripping — and the undisclosed common ownership removes any innocent reading. The detail worth internalising: no single transaction here looks odd. Each has an invoice and a plausible counterparty. Only the shape of the whole reveals it, which is why looking across transactions rather than at them is the core analytical habit.

consequences.close: A round-tripping structure left in place, with an unestablished beneficial owner in the chain.
consequences.escalate: Correct. Note that no individual transaction would have justified this — only the pattern.
consequences.rfi: You could ask for the deliverables, and their absence would be telling. But with circular flow and undisclosed common ownership already established, the case is made.

cases.title: Six deposits, one grieving customer
cases.customer: Ms L. Peeters · retail · customer since 2011
cases.narrative: Fourteen years of salary in, card spend out. Then six deposits between €8,000 and €9,600, all under the reporting threshold, across two branches. The pattern is textbook structuring. Textbook patterns have textbook explanations too.
cases.on_file: Cash deposits totalling €53,400 over eleven days on an account that has never seen cash. The rule fired on threshold proximity.
cases.law: AMLR Art. 69 — structuring is reportable; Art. 20 — CDD proportionate to risk. A pattern that matches a typology is a reason to ask, not a conclusion.
cases.why: Structuring detection is trivially easy to write and produces enormous noise. The skill is not spotting the pattern — the system did that. It is knowing which single question resolves it, and asking that one first.

consequences.close: The notarial deed makes the pattern explicable and the file defensible. Note what made this closeable: not the absence of a red flag — the flag was real and correctly raised — but a verified, documented explanation that reconciles with the amounts.
consequences.rfi: Reasonable, but you had the authority to ask directly. The RFI route adds a week and lands on someone else's desk.
consequences.escalate: Investigations will spend two days reaching the answer a single phone call would have produced. This is how queues stop working: not through laziness but through unwillingness to close.
consequences.sar: A report with no articulable suspicion behind it. Defensive filing degrades the intelligence the FIU receives, and it happened to a bereaved customer whose account may now be exited.

outcome_titles.rfi: Sent back for information you could have obtained

cases.epilogue_wrong: Three months later the customer moves her account. The complaint file notes she provided a notarial deed on request and was never told the outcome.

actions.name: Pull 24-month transaction history
actions.hint: Establish what normal looks like before deciding what abnormal means.

actions.name: Ask the customer for source of funds

e_tx.title: 24 months of history
e_tx.body: Salary of €3,180 monthly, card spend, one standing order. No cash activity of any size until 2 March. The six deposits are the only cash events in the entire period.

e_kyc.title: KYC file
e_kyc.body: Identity verified 2011 with Belgian ID, refreshed 2019. Occupation: nurse, university hospital. No corporate interests. Risk rating: low. Nothing has changed on the file.

e_rm.title: Relationship manager
e_rm.body: "She came in personally each time. Said she'd rather not carry it around. Her mother passed in January — I remember because she mentioned the funeral."

e_source.title: Source of funds — customer response
e_source.body: Customer provides a notarial succession deed dated 14 February. Estate included €54,000 held in cash in a safe deposit box, itemised in the inventory. Deposits total €53,400. She apologises for splitting them and says the branch advised her not to carry more than €10,000 at once.

e_media.title: Adverse media
e_media.body: No results. One namesake in a Dutch local newspaper, different age and city, unrelated.

e_peer.title: Peer group comparison
e_peer.body: Cash deposit behaviour is unusual for the salaried-professional segment, but the segment is broad and the comparison adds nothing the history has not already shown.

cases.title: Machinery that never leaves the port
cases.customer: Meridian Trading BVBA · corporate · high risk · customer since 2019
cases.narrative: The customer imports industrial parts and has done for six years. The payments are routine in shape. What is not routine is the intermediary that appeared four months ago, and the fact that the goods never touch the country billing for them.
cases.on_file: Four payments totalling €620,000 to a UAE intermediary for parts shipped directly from Pakistan. Invoice values look high.
cases.law: AMLR Art. 34 — EDD where a transaction has no apparent economic purpose; Art. 22 — beneficial ownership of counterparties; Art. 69 — reporting.
cases.why: Trade-based laundering hides inside legitimate commerce, which is why it is the most used and least detected typology. It is not visible in the transaction — it is visible in the price. Almost no bank benchmarks pricing, and that is precisely the gap being used.

consequences.close: Roughly €250,000 of unsupported value moved out through invoices you accepted at face value. The intermediary was a conduit and the pricing was the proof.
consequences.rfi: You have gone back to the party operating the structure and invited them to justify it. They will, plausibly, and the file will now contain their explanation as though it were evidence.
consequences.escalate: Defensible, and investigations will get there. But you had the two facts that make the case — pricing and ownership — and escalation without articulating them just moves the work.
consequences.sar: The report names what makes this suspicious: an intermediary handling no goods, systematic over-invoicing quantified against market, and a beneficial owner that cannot be established. That is a report an FIU analyst can act on.

outcome_titles.rfi: Asked the customer to explain their own scheme
outcome_titles.sar: Reported, with the value gap articulated

cases.epilogue_wrong: Eleven months later the FIU requests records for Meridian in connection with a sanctions-evasion network. The bank's file shows the alert was raised and dismissed without the pricing ever being checked.

actions.name: Establish beneficial ownership of the intermediary

e_tx.title: Payment history
e_tx.body: Six years of payments to eleven suppliers across Türkiye, Italy and Germany. Gulf Machinery FZE appears for the first time in December, and now accounts for 71% of outbound value.

e_invoice.title: The four invoices
e_invoice.body: Hydraulic control units, quantities 40–60 per shipment, unit prices between €3,100 and €3,900. Invoices are well formed. Terms: payment on issue, no retention.

e_price.title: Market price benchmark
e_price.body: Comparable hydraulic control units from three EU distributors: €1,850–€2,240. The invoiced prices sit 58–74% above the top of that range, consistently, across all four shipments. On €620,000 of payments, roughly €250,000 has no goods behind it.

e_ubo.title: Beneficial ownership of Gulf Machinery FZE
e_ubo.body: Incorporated four months ago. Sole corporate shareholder registered in a jurisdiction with no public register; nominee director provided by a corporate services firm. Beneficial owner cannot be established. One address match with a company previously owned by Meridian's own director.

e_ship.title: Shipping documentation
e_ship.body: Bills of lading show Karachi to Antwerp, direct. The UAE appears nowhere in the transport chain. The intermediary handles no goods.

e_media.title: Adverse media
e_media.body: Nothing on Meridian. Nothing on Gulf Machinery FZE — it is four months old and has no footprint at all, which is itself unremarkable for a new entity.

e_rm.title: Relationship manager
e_rm.body: "Good client, always pays, never a problem. They mentioned restructuring their supply chain for tax reasons. I didn't ask further."

e_credit.title: Credit file
e_credit.body: Facilities performing. No arrears. Turnover consistent with declared activity.

cases.title: Eleven accounts that behave like one
cases.customer: Retail cohort · payments institution · onboarded within 60 days
cases.narrative: One account: money in from strangers, money out within hours, balance returning to zero. Handled alone it is a small case. The question is whether it is alone.
cases.on_file: A single account flagged for pass-through activity. It does not look like much on its own.
cases.law: AMLR Art. 25 — ongoing monitoring; Art. 69 — reporting. TFR where onward transfers lack originator data.
cases.why: Mule networks are invisible one account at a time and obvious in aggregate. The decisive move is not deeper analysis of the flagged account — it is asking whether anything else behaves the same way. Most alert queues are structured to prevent exactly that question.

consequences.close: The single account was small. The network was not. Victim funds continued to move through the other ten for as long as they stayed open.
consequences.rfi: Beyond the delay, this risks tipping off the network operating the accounts — and the answer would not have changed what the transaction data already showed.
consequences.escalate: Correct instinct on the account in front of you. But if you escalated without the cohort, investigations receive one small case rather than a network, and the other ten stay open.
consequences.sar: Eleven linked accounts, a shared device fingerprint, common destinations and identified victim funds. This is a report that lets an FIU see a structure rather than an incident.

outcome_titles.close: Closed one account and left ten running

cases.epilogue_wrong: Four months later, three of the remaining accounts appear in a police request. Total victim losses routed through the institution during the intervening period: €338,000.

actions.name: Look for accounts with the same behavioural signature
Check device and IP overlap across accounts
Adverse media on the account holder

e_tx.title: Flagged account
e_tx.body: €47,200 in from twelve unrelated private senders over nine days, €46,850 out to three accounts in Poland, Lithuania and Romania. Holder is 21, declared a student job at onboarding.

e_cohort.title: Behavioural cohort
e_cohort.body: Eleven accounts share the signature: onboarded within a 60-day window, dormant 2–3 weeks, then pass-through activity of €40k–€60k each. Aggregate €512,000. Nine of the eleven send onward to the same three destination accounts.

e_device.title: Device and IP overlap
e_device.body: Seven of the eleven accounts were opened from the same device fingerprint. Four share an IP block used during onboarding but never afterwards. The account holders do not appear to know each other.

e_onboard.title: Onboarding records
e_onboard.body: All eleven passed identity verification with genuine documents. The identities are real. The holders are real. Nothing in onboarding failed.

e_victim.title: Fraud cross-reference
e_victim.body: Nineteen of the inbound senders across the cohort appear in fraud complaints — investment scams and marketplace fraud. Funds are victim proceeds.

e_ask.title: Contact the account holder
e_ask.body: No response to two attempts. Note: contacting a suspected mule risks tipping off the network operating the accounts, and the transaction record already establishes the pattern.

e_media.title: Adverse media
e_media.body: Nothing. Twenty-one-year-old with no public footprint.

cases.title: A shareholder just under the line
cases.customer: Northwind Logistics NV · corporate · customer since 2016
cases.narrative: Nothing has fired. The relationship manager flagged this himself: the customer restructured its shareholding three months ago and the new holders sit conspicuously below every threshold that would have triggered anything.
cases.on_file: A long-standing customer changes its ownership structure. Screening returns no hits.
cases.law: EU Regulation 269/2014 — asset freezes extend to entities owned or controlled by designated persons; AMLR Art. 22 — beneficial ownership; Art. 34 — EDD.
cases.why: Sanctions screening matches names on the record in front of it. A structure built two levels up will never appear there. The 50% rule aggregates across chains and the control limb applies regardless of percentage — which means the only reliable defence is looking through the chain, and almost nobody does it unprompted.

consequences.close: The screening returned nothing because the designated person was never on the customer's record. The structure was built precisely to produce that result, and it worked.
consequences.rfi: The structure was designed to be asked about. You will receive a coherent, documented answer that confirms the surface facts you already have.
consequences.escalate: Right that this needed to leave your desk. But a sanctions nexus is not an ordinary escalation — asset-freeze obligations bite immediately, and the timing of the report matters.
consequences.sar: You identified what the screening could not: that no single holding breaches a threshold, that the aggregate does, and that control sits with parties connected to a designated individual. This is the case sanctions screening is structurally unable to find on its own.

outcome_titles.rfi: Asked the customer about its own ownership
outcome_titles.sar: Reported, with the aggregation set out

cases.epilogue_wrong: Fourteen months later the structure surfaces in an EU enforcement action. The institution's exposure is characterised as a failure to look through a chain that was, on the record, visible from the documents it already held.

actions.name: Screen every entity in the chain, not just the customer
Review transaction flows since the restructure

e_struct.title: Ownership map
e_struct.body: Three new corporate shareholders replaced the previous single holder: Baltic Freight OÜ (24%), Anchor Marine Ltd (23%), Verda Holdings Sàrl (22%). Remaining 31% held by the original founder. No single holder above 25%.

e_aggregate.title: Aggregated ownership
e_aggregate.body: Baltic Freight OÜ and Anchor Marine Ltd are both ultimately majority-owned by the same designated individual. Combined: 47%. Under the 50% rule the designated person does not control Northwind — but combined with Verda, in which he holds a 40% stake, indirect economic interest reaches 55.8%.

e_sanc.title: Chain-wide screening
e_sanc.body: Screening the customer returns nothing. Screening every entity in the chain returns a designated individual two levels up, listed under EU Regulation 269/2014 since 2022. He appears nowhere on the customer's own record.

e_control.title: Control rights
e_control.body: The shareholders' agreement grants Baltic and Anchor jointly the right to appoint three of five board members and a veto over asset disposals. Control exists independently of the percentages.

e_tx.title: Flows since the restructure
e_tx.body: Freight receipts unchanged in pattern. One new payment corridor to a jurisdiction the customer has not previously traded with, €340,000 across four payments.

e_media.title: Adverse media
e_media.body: Two trade-press articles on the restructure, describing it as a management buy-in. No mention of the ultimate holder.

e_rm.title: Relationship manager
e_rm.body: "They told me it was a succession plan. I thought it was odd that three buyers appeared at once, which is why I raised it. That's as far as my knowledge goes."

e_legal.title: Restructuring documents
e_legal.body: Share purchase agreements executed on the same day, before the same notary, with sequential document numbers. The three transactions were not independent.

cases.title: A director with a familiar surname
cases.customer: Meridiaan Ventures NV · corporate onboarding · new relationship
cases.narrative: New corporate account application for Meridiaan Ventures NV, an import/export trading firm. PEP screening on the listed director, Koen Verstraeten, returns a potential match to a former provincial deputy (gedeputeerde) of the same name who served until 2019. Onboarding is on hold pending your review.
cases.on_file: Screening hit generated at onboarding, before any account activity. No transactions yet.
cases.law: AMLR Art. 36 — enhanced due diligence for PEPs, family members and known close associates; Art. 37 — senior management approval and source of wealth verification before entering the relationship.
cases.why: PEP status is a factor, not a verdict. The law doesn't ask you to decline a PEP relationship — it asks you to understand where the money comes from and get someone senior to sign off knowing what you know. Declining removes the friction of doing that work; escalating sends a routine EDD case to a queue built for suspected crime, not for onboarding risk.

consequences.close: You declined a legal relationship because the screening hit was uncomfortable, not because anything on file justified it. If Meridiaan Ventures NV re-applies elsewhere, this bank has no record of why — only that it walked away from a PEP without documenting a reason.
consequences.rfi: Right. Identity match confirmed, the public role understood, source of wealth verified and documented before terms were agreed.
consequences.escalate: Investigations opens a file for a customer who has committed no offence and shows no red flag beyond the PEP hit itself. The case sits behind genuinely suspicious activity while someone re-does the EDD you could have done directly.
consequences.sar: There is no suspicion here to report — a PEP match with a clean, documented source of wealth is exactly what EDD is designed to clear. Filing anyway trains the FIU to expect noise from your desk.

cases.epilogue_wrong: Three weeks later, Meridiaan Ventures NV opens with a competitor bank instead — whose file notes a straightforward EDD review with no findings. Compliance asks why this desk declined first and documented second.

e_sow.body: Verstraeten provides a summary of pension income, rental income from two properties (deeds attached), and proceeds from the 2020 sale of his shareholding in a family construction firm (sale contract attached). e_ubo.body: Two other directors, neither a PEP nor a PEP associate. Verstraeten holds 40% of shares; the remaining 60% is split between his two adult children — not PEPs themselves, but close family of one.

e_media.body: No adverse media. One local news mention of a 2017 zoning dispute, resolved administratively — not a corruption allegation.

e_policy.body: PEP relationships require EDD — verified source of wealth, senior management approval, annual review — but are not prohibited. A former regional PEP with no adverse media and a documented source of wealth does not meet the decline threshold.

cases.title: A wire to a name on the list
cases.customer: Corporate · Dunmore Trading SA · customer since 2016 · standard risk
cases.narrative: An outbound wire of €118,000 to a supplier, "Petrov Logistics OOD" (Bulgaria), triggers a sanctions screening alert: the beneficiary name is a fuzzy match against "Petrov Holdings" — an entity 60% owned by a person on the EU consolidated list. The payment is held pending review.
cases.on_file: First payment to this beneficiary. Dunmore Trading SA has an established freight-forwarding relationship with several Eastern European suppliers.
cases.law: Regulation (EU) 2580/2001 and successor sanctions regimes — the 50% rule: an entity is treated as designated if a listed person owns or controls it above 50%, directly or in aggregate. A screening hit must be resolved to a documented conclusion before funds move.
cases.why: A fuzzy name match is a reason to look, not a reason to block or a reason to wave through. The screening system did its job — it surfaced a hit that needed a human to resolve. The skill here isn't reacting to the alert; it's establishing, on the actual ownership evidence, whether this is the listed entity or a company that merely shares part of a common name.

consequences.close: Right. Ownership pulled, ultimate control established below the 50% threshold with no designated person in the chain, and the release documented against that evidence — not against a hunch.
consequences.rfi: You asked Dunmore Trading SA to explain a payment to their own supplier instead of checking the supplier's ownership yourself — the information was available directly and faster.
consequences.escalate: Defensible caution, but the ownership registry answered this in minutes. Investigations re-ran the same public-registry check you had access to.
consequences.sar: You reported a payment between two unconnected private companies because their names partially overlapped. The FIU received a filing with no sanctions nexus behind it.

outcome_titles.rfi: Sent the question to the wrong party
outcome_titles.sar: Reported a false positive as suspicious

cases.epilogue_wrong: The held payment triggers a formal complaint from Dunmore Trading SA over the delay to a routine supplier invoice — compliance asks to see the ownership check that justified holding it this long.

cases.rule: Private banking · large deposit · SoW/SoF review
cases.title: A consultant's very good year
cases.customer: Private banking · Ms I. Vandenberghe · EDD relationship · self-employed consultant
cases.narrative: Existing EDD private banking client wants to deposit €800,000, described on the transfer instruction as “proceeds from sale of property abroad.” Her file already documents a plausible overall wealth story — a successful 20-year management consulting practice. The relationship manager has pre-approved the deposit on that basis and asks you to sign off before it lands.
cases.on_file: Client's annual EDD review (completed four months ago) describes her as a high-earning independent consultant, net worth estimated at €1.2–1.5M, built over two decades. No property assets were listed on that review.
cases.law: AMLR Art. 22 — identification of the source of funds for the specific transaction, distinct from Art. 20's assessment of overall source of wealth. A plausible SoW does not discharge the SoF requirement for an individual transaction.
cases.why: Source of wealth explains a person. Source of funds explains a transaction. The relationship manager's sign-off answers the first question — she is, generally, someone who could plausibly have €800,000. It does not answer the second: did this €800,000 actually come from a property sale, as stated, or from somewhere else entirely. Those are different questions and one does not stand in for the other.

consequences.close: You accepted a specific, checkable claim — “proceeds from a property sale” — without checking it, on the strength of a general wealth narrative that was never about this transaction. If the stated origin is false, the file now shows a professional who saw the gap and signed anyway.
consequences.rfi: Right. Sale deed and transfer confirmation requested and matched to the amount and date — the specific claim is now evidence, not narrative.
consequences.escalate: Defensible — investigations can request the same documentation — but this was a same-day evidentiary gap you had the standing to close directly, not a judgement call requiring a second opinion.
consequences.sar: Filed on a client with an unverified but entirely plausible transaction, before asking a single question that would likely have resolved it. Premature reporting on a routine documentation gap.

outcome_titles.close: Signed off on wealth, not on funds
outcome_titles.rfi: Source of funds verified against the specific claim
outcome_titles.sar: Reported before verifying a checkable claim

cases.epilogue_wrong: An unrelated review six months later turns up no record of any foreign property ever owned by the client. The €800,000 origin was never established — and the file that accepted it carries your sign-off.

e_media.body: No adverse media on the client. No results for either party to the transaction.
